hints: Think of $K_{stab}$ like a $K_c$ for formation of the complex from the free metal ion and free ligands, then count how many $en$ molecules are needed to make one $[\text{Ni}(en)_3]^{2+}$.
walkthrough:
Recall what Kstab means**
Think of $K_{\text{stab}}$ as the equilibrium constant for building the complex. You start from free $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ (or $[\text{Ni}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$ with water omitted) plus free $en$ ligands, and you end with $[\text{Ni}(en)_3]^{2+}$. Products go on top, reactants go on the bottom, just like $K_c$.

Apply the 1 to 3 stoichiometry**
One $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ needs three $en$ molecules to give $[\text{Ni}(en)_3]^{2+}$. So the bottom must have $[\text{Ni}^{2+}]$ to the power 1 and $[en]$ to the power 3: $$K_{\text{stab}} = \frac{[[\text{Ni}(en)_3]^{2+}]}{[\text{Ni}^{2+}][en]^3}$$

hints: Compare the two $K_{\text{stab}}$ values in Table 5.1 at the same ligand concentrations and remember that a larger $K_{\text{stab}}$ means the equilibrium lies much further toward the complex.
walkthrough:
Let the numbers decide**
You have $0.10 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ of each ligand, so concentration does not give either side an advantage. Look at Table 5.1: $4.8 \times 10^{7}$ for $[\text{Ni}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{2+}$ but $2.0 \times 10^{18}$ for $[\text{Ni}(en)_3]^{2+}$. That is about $10^{11}$ times larger.

Link larger Kstab to more product**
A larger $K_{\text{stab}}$ means a more stable complex and an equilibrium position much further to the right. So $en$ outcompetes $\text{NH}_3$ for $\text{Ni}^{2+}$, and $[\text{Ni}(en)_3]^{2+}$ dominates in the mixture.

Final answer: complex ion present in largest concentration = $[\text{Ni}(en)_3]^{2+}$
explanation: $K_{\text{stab}}$ for $[\text{Ni}(en)_3]^{2+}$ is much larger ($2.0 \times 10^{18}$ vs $4.8 \times 10^{7}$), so it is more stable and formation is more favoured.

hints: Start from $[\text{Ni}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$ and remember each $en$ is bidentate and replaces two water molecules, so work out how many $en$ and how many $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ balance the six coordination sites.
walkthrough:
Balance the coordination sites**
$\text{Ni}^{2+}$ is six coordinate and octahedral. Each $en$, $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$, is bidentate and occupies two sites through its two N atoms. To replace six $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ molecules you need three $en$ molecules.

Write the complete exchange**
Keep the $\text{Ni}$ and charge balanced, and release all displaced water: $$[\text{Ni}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+} + 3en \rightarrow [\text{Ni}(en)_3]^{2+} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

hints: Recall that $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ with three bidentate ligands is still six coordinate and octahedral, with each N-N arch joining two adjacent (cis) positions, not opposite ends.
Think of the three $en$ arches arranged like the blades of a propeller which can twist clockwise or anticlockwise to give two non-superimposable forms.
Decide what type of stereoisomerism gives non-superimposable mirror images with no plane of symmetry in an octahedral complex.
walkthrough:
Set up the octahedral framework**
Picture $\text{Ni}$ in the centre with six bonds pointing to the corners of an octahedron. Each $en$ is shown as N with an arch to N, and each arch must span two neighbouring positions at 90 degrees to each other. It cannot span straight across the metal from top to bottom.

Draw the first propeller**
Draw one $en$ vertically behind the Ni, one $en$ to the left front, and one $en$ to the right front, using solid wedges for bonds coming out and hashed wedges for bonds going back to show 3D shape. This gives one twisted arrangement, like a three-bladed propeller turning one way.

Draw its mirror image**
Now draw the exact mirror reflection of that arrangement. The arches twist the opposite way. Try to rotate one to fit exactly on top of the other in your mind and you will find you cannot superimpose them, just like left and right hands. These are the pair of enantiomers.

Name the isomerism**
Because the two structures are non-superimposable mirror images, this is optical isomerism. $[\text{Ni}(en)_3]^{2+}$ shows no cis-trans or fac-mer isomerism here, only this pair of optical isomers which would rotate plane polarised light in opposite directions.

Final answer: Two 3D octahedral structures, each with Ni at centre and three N-N ($en$) arches occupying cis pairs of sites, drawn as non-superimposable mirror images (one left-handed propeller, one right-handed propeller).
type of isomerism shown: optical isomerism
